evidence.supportingExcerpt: Cytokines are signalling proteins whose binding to a suitable receptor changes signalling and gene expression in a receiving cell. Autocrine action is on the producing cell, paracrine action is on neighbours, and endocrine action is at a distance, for example after entry into the circulation. Distant action is possible rather than the default for every cytokine (British Society for Immunology, Cytokines: Introduction). Chemokines are a cytokine family involved in cell recruitment and can also affect leukocyte activation (NLM MeSH, Chemokines). The information-versus-fuel distinction is a reading rule: a measured amount of signalling protein does not measure the energy available to the cell, and a message without the relevant receptor and response machinery does not establish a response.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: A synthetic cytokine receptor is an engineered cell-surface protein that connects a specified input to intracellular signalling. It differs from engineering a soluble cytokine or simply administering a cytokine. Some designs require an externally supplied ligand; others generate ligand-independent signalling. The receptor domains, input, expression and cell type define the tested construct. A growth-supporting signal does not itself establish antigen recognition, entry into a tumour, completed killing or durable patient benefit.

Engelowski and colleagues joined fluorescent-protein-binding nanobodies to selected cytokine-receptor membrane and intracellular domains. Artificial GFP/mCherry-based ligands induced signalling in experimental systems. That 2018 study is a particular ligand-dependent design, not a test of every synthetic receptor or of a company platform with a different architecture.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: In a 2010 human T-cell study, a chimeric receptor joined the IL-4 receptor binding region to an IL-2/IL-15 receptor signalling component. IL-4 supported expansion of the engineered cells, while a separate CAR specified the tumour target. The reported culture experiments distinguished expansion, cytokine dependence and target-cell killing; they were not patient efficacy results.

Read each supportive feature as a testable hypothesis. A drug-triggered signal needs a baseline and a withdrawal test; an antigen-triggered signal needs testing after cells leave the priming site. Constitutive signalling raises different growth and cell-state questions, while a secreted payload can affect neighbouring cells or circulate. Orthogonal means sufficiently separate from natural partners under tested conditions, not selectivity established by its name. The supportive receptor does not specify the CAR target, and changing an internal signal is different from secreting a cytokine. An added support signal does not by itself demonstrate adequate oxygen, tissue access, recognition of an absent antigen or patient benefit.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: For a drug-gated construct, withdrawing the input can reduce a selected signal without eliminating cells already engineered. Receptor signalling, viable-cell counts, tissue location, target-cell killing and later disease control need distinct measurements. A growth or activity switch is different from a cell-elimination mechanism.

A living cell product can persist after administration stops. Activity switches regulate a defined function; elimination switches aim to remove cells. A drug-gated receptor may require a supplied molecule for signaling, whereas inducible caspase-9 activates a cell-death pathway when its dimerizing trigger is given. A removable surface tag offers another clearance route. These mechanisms need evidence within the actual finished product, including trigger exposure, speed, completeness and residual activity. None guarantees instant removal from every tissue or reversal of prior injury.

Di Stasi tested inducible caspase-9 in donor T cells after haploidentical stem-cell transplantation, rather than as a general CAR-T rescue trial. In the GD2-CART01 neuroblastoma report, the suicide switch was activated in one participant.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: CAR-T cell therapy uses T cells carrying a chimeric antigen receptor to recognize a target. FDA-approved products include CD19- and BCMA-directed CAR-T cells for selected blood cancers, including B-cell leukemias, lymphomas and multiple myeloma. The individual product label defines the treatment setting and eligibility. A common autologous approach collects a person’s T cells, engineers and expands them outside the body, then infuses them back; conditioning and follow-up depend on the protocol.

The June 2026 Tecelra label names HLA-A*02:01P, -A*02:02P, -A*02:03P and -A*02:06P and a MAGE-A4 tumor test in its indication, with a separate HLA-A*02:05P contraindication. The approval letter documents the adult conversion and pediatric expansion. These are product-specific regulatory scopes, not a general rule for every TCR-T.

In a fictional tumour sample, 70 of 100 cells display an epitope accessible to the proposed receptor and 30 do not. A second target has only an RNA result, while healthy tissue was stained with a third antibody. Those measurements cannot rank safe receptor designs: ask for the actual binder’s recognition, the unrecognised tumour population and functional effects on relevant healthy cells. A more sensitive receptor might recognise additional tumour cells and additional healthy cells. Even a perfectly specific binder can harm healthy cells carrying its intended antigen; unintended binding to another molecule is a different failure. A sampled panel can miss antigen-negative cells, and an intracellular signal does not establish an accessible surface epitope. Repeat the relevant healthy-cell question under conditions, including inflammation, that could change recognition.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: For interpretation, report the parent population, percentage and any valid absolute count with the specimen and sampling method. Receptor-sequence abundance does not identify the receptor ligand. Rigau et al. (2020) established a defined BTN2A1-dependent recognition mechanism for the Vgamma9Vdelta2 phosphoantigen response; that specificity is an example of why innate-like does not mean nonspecific. To test native versus added-receptor recognition, compare matched cells without the added receptor, target-positive and target-negative cells, and a suitable receptor-blocking or target-perturbation condition. Keep relevant healthy-cell controls, viability and exposure conditions explicit. This is experimental-design reasoning from the separate recognition mechanisms, not a claim that one cited assay validates every product. HLA loss does not establish that the native ligand or the added receptor target is present, and two recognition routes do not prove escape prevention.

In a fictional target cell, HLA allele A is lost while B remains. An A-restricted receptor loses that route; a B-restricted receptor still needs its own peptide to be processed and displayed. B2M is the shared light chain for many class-I complexes, whereas class-II HLA uses different alpha and beta chains. Neither one lost allele nor a change in interferon-induced display establishes complete loss of baseline presentation. Test the required allele, antigen and display conditions with matched viable targets rather than infer recognition from the HLA label. A conventional surface-antigen CAR has another dependency, and reduced class I alone does not guarantee NK-cell killing.

semanticAssessment.explanation: HLA/B2M changes do not supply a native or engineered ligand and do not by themselves establish killing or benefit.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: Conventional alpha-beta TCR-T introduces selected paired receptor-chain instructions into therapeutic T cells. The receptor recognizes a displayed peptide-HLA complex, rather than entering the tumor cell to bind the whole source protein. Natural processing, the required HLA allele, surface display, receptor expression and useful cell function remain different questions. This differs from administering a soluble TCR/CD3 protein that recruits other T cells.

Cameron investigated fatal cardiac toxicity with one affinity-enhanced MAGE-A3 receptor and identified a cross-reactive Titin peptide presented by HLA-A*01 as the most likely cause. Earlier screening had not detected the hazard. This was a different receptor from the MAGE-A4 product Tecelra; stronger binding does not establish improved specificity or safety for either a new construct or an entire family.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: Recognition differs by subset, and it is not always free of HLA. For the Vγ9Vδ2 subset, which responds to phosphoantigens (small phosphorylated metabolites produced by microbes and overexpressed by some cancers), butyrophilin 2A1 (BTN2A1) binds the Vγ9 chain of the receptor, associates with a second butyrophilin, BTN3A1, and the two act together to start the response; a second ligand, possibly BTN3A1, binds a separate region that includes the Vδ2 chain (Rigau et al., 2020). This is not a peptide sitting in an HLA groove. HLA independence is also not universal: one characterised Vγ5Vδ1 receptor was restricted by HLA-A*24:02 and depended on the CD8-alpha co-receptor, acting on blood-cancer and solid-tumour cells in vitro and in vivo while sparing healthy tissue in those models (Kierkels et al., 2019). That receptor's mechanism is not an eligibility rule for the family.

Recognition varies by subset and receptor. Some routes do not use classical peptide-HLA presentation, while an HLA-restricted gamma-delta receptor has also been described. The family name therefore does not establish universal freedom from HLA requirements, tissue matching or graft-versus-host disease. Native recognition, added-receptor function, tumour entry, persistence and clinical outcomes need separate evidence.

The gamma-delta T-cell receptor, NKG2D and DNAM-1 are different receptors. BTN2A1 binds the Vgamma9 receptor chain and works with BTN3A1 in the specified phosphoantigen response; the BTN names do not name the T-cell receptor itself. Reviewed human UniProt entries distinguish NKG2D ligands, including MICA, MICB and ULBP proteins, from the DNAM-1/CD226 ligands CD155/PVR and CD112/NECTIN2. These receptor-ligand associations do not establish that every gamma-delta subset expresses or uses each route. Check the actual cell preparation and keep ligand identity, receptor expression and controlled target-cell killing separate.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: An engineered receptor is a separate recognition route. Adding a GD2-directed chimeric antigen receptor to expanded human Vδ1 and Vδ2 cells increased GD2-specific killing of GD2-expressing cancer cell lines, did not impair movement towards tumour cells in vitro, and expanded Vδ2 cells kept the ability to take up tumour antigen and cross-present it to alpha-beta T cells (Capsomidis et al., 2018). That is a preclinical result for that preparation, and it does not show that any gamma-delta product enters tumours, cross-presents usefully or prevents antigen escape in patients. An allogeneic gamma-delta product that the registry names HLA-G-CAR.BiTE allogeneic γδ T cells (NCT06150885, phase 1 and 2) was listed as recruiting when the registry record was read for this entry; the record describes the product and the study design and reports no efficacy. A receptor added to a cell needs its own target on the tumour, HLA-low does not mean target-positive, and avoiding peptide presentation is not the same as avoiding antigen escape. Cells are identified by flow cytometry and receptor sequencing, but a response against one target line does not establish tumour entry, persistence or benefit, and matched cells without the added receptor are needed to separate native from engineered recognition. Two cautions are OnCo's reasoning and not findings of the cited papers: a product made of many receptor clones is not automatically broader or more effective than one defined clone, and the name gamma-delta describes the receptor chains and not the cell source, so whether cells came from the patient or from a donor has to be stated separately.

For interpretation, report the parent population, percentage and any valid absolute count with the specimen and sampling method. Receptor-sequence abundance does not identify the receptor ligand. Rigau et al. (2020) established a defined BTN2A1-dependent recognition mechanism for the Vgamma9Vdelta2 phosphoantigen response; that specificity is an example of why innate-like does not mean nonspecific. To test native versus added-receptor recognition, compare matched cells without the added receptor, target-positive and target-negative cells, and a suitable receptor-blocking or target-perturbation condition. Keep relevant healthy-cell controls, viability and exposure conditions explicit. This is experimental-design reasoning from the separate recognition mechanisms, not a claim that one cited assay validates every product. HLA loss does not establish that the native ligand or the added receptor target is present, and two recognition routes do not prove escape prevention.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: Recognition varies by subset and receptor. Some routes do not use classical peptide-HLA presentation, while an HLA-restricted gamma-delta receptor has also been described. The family name therefore does not establish universal freedom from HLA requirements, tissue matching or graft-versus-host disease. Native recognition, added-receptor function, tumour entry, persistence and clinical outcomes need separate evidence.

Rigau identified BTN2A1 as a ligand for the Vgamma9 T-cell-receptor chain, acting with BTN3A1 in the Vgamma9Vdelta2 phosphoantigen response. Kierkels instead characterised a Vgamma5Vdelta1 receptor requiring HLA-A*24:02 and CD8-alpha in cell and mouse experiments. These are different recognition mechanisms, not a universal matching or safety rule. Capsomidis added a GD2 CAR to expanded human Vdelta1 and Vdelta2 preparations and observed enhanced GD2-specific cancer-cell-line killing; migration and cross-presentation were separately tested. Those preclinical results do not establish clinical benefit or absence of graft-versus-host disease for every gamma-delta product.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: Targeted delivery can supply CAR-encoding instructions to cells inside the body, using formats such as a viral vector or an mRNA lipid nanoparticle. This changes where engineering happens; it does not mean the active cells are donor-derived. Delivery targeting, cancer-antigen recognition, generated-cell abundance, receptor duration and useful function are separate questions. Conditioning, repeat dosing, safety and total cost belong to a specified product and protocol rather than to the in vivo label.

A carrier delivers a genetic payload. Transduction is vector-mediated gene transfer; integration places DNA in a chromosome; expression produces an encoded RNA or protein. These are different events. Follow the causal chain in separate steps: administered carrier, distribution and cell contact, entry and usable cargo release, expression in identified cells, survival or expansion and movement, then recognition and effects in tumour and healthy tissue. Fluorescent uptake need not mean useful expression, and detecting two components somewhere in a sample does not show that the same cells express both. A carrier-lot aliquot, a timed blood sample and a tissue biopsy answer different questions. Sequence copies, viable receptor-positive fractions and controlled killing cannot substitute for one another or supply a universal release threshold. A carrier name does not determine its administration route. FDA’s CAR T-cell guidance focuses on ex vivo products; its principles do not by themselves validate a release specification for an in vivo carrier.

A fictional receptor kills X-positive tumour cells and normal airway cells that also display X: that is the on-target, off-tumour problem. If it also recognises Y on an X-negative healthy cell, that is off-target cross-reactivity. Binding or surface contact does not itself measure injury. Record tissue, assay sensitivity, staining intensity, positive fraction or calibrated molecules per cell, binding specificity, and healthy-cell killing or cytokine release at a named time; viable-cell tests consume the sample. Clinical organ injury is a further outcome in the actual population and regimen. A staining ratio, one negative panel or a control switch does not establish safety everywhere or guarantee reversal of an injury already present.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: For a nuclear protein-coding gene in a eukaryotic cell, transcription occurs in the nucleus and the message reaches cytoplasmic ribosomes for translation. A delivered messenger RNA can begin at cytoplasmic translation without requiring genomic integration. This does not imply an empty nucleus or removal of existing nuclear DNA. Neither DNA nor an untranslated message is itself the finished receptor protein. Translation alone does not establish correct folding, processing, transport or function at the cell surface.

A receptor-bearing cell, its genetic instructions and its receptor protein are different objects. Killing the X-positive 80 leaves 20 survivors; ten times as many effector cells does not create X on them. For two targets, suppose 20 cells carry both X and Y, 60 carry X only, ten Y only and ten neither. An idealised either-target rule covers 90 cells, whereas a both-target rule covers 20. These are recognition-coverage calculations, not measured killing or healthy-tissue selectivity. Expression thresholds, tissue access and cell function still matter.

A fictional receptor kills X-positive tumour cells and normal airway cells that also display X: that is the on-target, off-tumour problem. If it also recognises Y on an X-negative healthy cell, that is off-target cross-reactivity. Binding or surface contact does not itself measure injury. Record tissue, assay sensitivity, staining intensity, positive fraction or calibrated molecules per cell, binding specificity, and healthy-cell killing or cytokine release at a named time; viable-cell tests consume the sample. Clinical organ injury is a further outcome in the actual population and regimen. A staining ratio, one negative panel or a control switch does not establish safety everywhere or guarantee reversal of an injury already present.

evidence.supportingExcerpt: The fictional mouse card compares administered carrier P with empty carrier, with D in both arms and six mice per arm. One selected day-seven blood sample has 120 dual-positive cells among 200 T cells, or 60 per cent; this is not the six-mouse denominator, and two treated biopsies contain few engineered cells. Mean tumour volume is stated as 100 cubic millimetres at baseline, then 300 for P and 1,000 for control at day 28. P is 70 per cent smaller than control but three times the stated baseline: reduced growth, not regression below baseline or cure. Later follow-up, spread and causes of poor entry are missing. Without a matched CAR-X-without-R mouse arm, the comparison cannot isolate R’s contribution or establish every animal’s outcome.

For the fictional growth example, the percentage smaller than the final control is 100 times (control endpoint minus treated endpoint) divided by the control endpoint. The fold from baseline is the treated endpoint divided by baseline. Keep these two comparisons separate: a favourable control comparison can accompany growth from baseline. These ratios require finite, non-negative volumes and positive baseline and control denominators. They are not a baseline-adjusted growth-inhibition formula or a clinical response classification. An upper input limit in a teaching calculator is a property of that exercise, not a biological threshold.
